**Joseph Hall** (1 July 1574 – 8 September 1656) was an [English bishop](/wiki/List_of_bishops_in_the_Church_of_England "List of bishops in the Church of England"), [satirist](/wiki/Satire "Satire") and [moralist](/wiki/Moralism "Moralism"). His contemporaries knew him as a devotional writer, and a high-profile [controversialist](/wiki/Polemic "Polemic") of the early 1640s. In church politics, he tended in fact to a middle way.

[Thomas Fuller](/wiki/Thomas_Fuller "Thomas Fuller") wrote:[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1)

> He was commonly called our English Seneca, for the purenesse, plainnesse, and fulnesse of his style. Not unhappy at Controversies, more happy at Comments, very good in his Characters, better in his Sermons, best of all in his Meditations.

Hall's relationship to the [stoicism](/wiki/Stoicism "Stoicism") of the [classical age](/wiki/Classical_antiquity "Classical antiquity"), exemplified by [Seneca the Younger](/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger "Seneca the Younger"), is still debated, with the importance of [neo-stoicism](/wiki/Neo-stoicism "Neo-stoicism") and the influence of the [Flemish](/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") philosopher [Justus Lipsius](/wiki/Justus_Lipsius "Justus Lipsius") to his work being contested, in contrast to [Christian morality](/wiki/Christian_ethics "Christian ethics").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChew19501130–1145-2)

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Joseph Hall was born at Bristow Park, [Ashby-de-la-Zouch](/wiki/Ashby-de-la-Zouch "Ashby-de-la-Zouch"), on 1 July 1574. His father John Hall was employed under [Henry Hastings, 3rd Earl of Huntingdon](/wiki/Henry_Hastings,_3rd_Earl_of_Huntingdon "Henry Hastings, 3rd Earl of Huntingdon"), president of the north, and was his deputy at Ashby. His mother was Winifred Bambridge, a strict puritan ([Perry 1890](#CITEREFPerry1890), p. 75),[[a]](#cite_note-3) whom her son compared to St. Monica.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)

Hall attended [Ashby Grammar School](/wiki/Ashby_Grammar_School "Ashby Grammar School"). When he was 15, Mr. Pelset, lecturer at Leicester, a divine of puritan views, offered to take him "under indentures" and educate him for the ministry. Just before this arrangement was completed, it came to the knowledge of Nathaniel Gilby, son of [Anthony Gilby](/wiki/Anthony_Gilby "Anthony Gilby") and a fellow of [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge"), who was a friend of the family. Gilby induced Hall's father to send his son to Emmanuel College in 1589. The expense of his education at the university was partly borne by his uncle, Edmund Sleigh. He was elected scholar and afterwards fellow of Emmanuel College (1595), graduating B.A. in 1592 and M.A. in 1596 (B.D. 1603 and D.D. 1612).([Perry 1890](#CITEREFPerry1890), p. 75) Fuller, nearly a contemporary, says that Hall "passed all his degrees with great applause".([Perry 1890](#CITEREFPerry1890), p. 75) He obtained a high reputation in the university for scholarship, and read the public rhetoric lecture in the schools for two years with much credit.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189075-5)[[5]](#cite_note-6)

Priesthood
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Priesthood")]

Having taken [holy orders](/wiki/Holy_orders "Holy orders"), Hall was offered the mastership of [Blundell's School](/wiki/Blundell%27s_School "Blundell's School"), [Tiverton](/wiki/Tiverton,_Devon "Tiverton, Devon"), but he refused it in favour of the living of [Hawstead](/wiki/Hawstead "Hawstead"), Suffolk, to which he was presented (1601) by [Sir Robert Drury](/wiki/Robert_Drury_(17th_century_MP) "Robert Drury (17th century MP)"). The appointment was not wholly satisfactory: in his parish Hall had an opponent in a Mr Lilly, whom he describes as a "witty and bold atheist",[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) he had to find money to make his house habitable, and he felt that his patron Sir Robert underpaid him. Nevertheless, in 1603, he married Elizabeth Wynniff of Brettenham, Suffolk (see "[Family](#Family)" below).[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)

In 1605, Hall travelled abroad for the first time when he accompanied Sir [Edmund Bacon](/wiki/Sir_Edmund_Bacon,_2nd_Baronet,_of_Redgrave "Sir Edmund Bacon, 2nd Baronet, of Redgrave") on an embassy to [Spa](/wiki/Spa,_Belgium "Spa, Belgium"), with the special aim, he says, of acquainting himself with the state and practice of the Roman Catholic Church. At [Brussels](/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), he disputed at the [Jesuit](/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit") college on the authenticity of modern miracles, until his patron at length asked him to stop.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)

Hall's devotional writings had attracted the notice of [Henry, Prince of Wales](/wiki/Henry_Frederick,_Prince_of_Wales "Henry Frederick, Prince of Wales"), who made him one of his chaplains (1608).[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) Hall preached officially on the tenth anniversary of [King James's](/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") accession in 1613, with an assessment in *An Holy Panegyrick* of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") flattering to the king.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParry1981232–235-7)

In 1612, [Edward Denny](/wiki/Edward_Denny,_1st_Earl_of_Norwich "Edward Denny, 1st Earl of Norwich") gave Hall the [curacy](/wiki/Curacy "Curacy") of [Waltham Holy Cross](/wiki/Waltham_Holy_Cross "Waltham Holy Cross"), Essex, and, in the same year, he received the degree of [D.D.](/wiki/D.D. "D.D.") Later he received the [prebend](/wiki/Prebendary "Prebendary") of [Willenhall](/wiki/Willenhall "Willenhall") in [St Peter's](/wiki/St_Peter%27s_Collegiate_Church "St Peter's Collegiate Church"), the [collegiate church](/wiki/Collegiate_church "Collegiate church") of [Wolverhampton](/wiki/Wolverhampton "Wolverhampton"), and, in 1616, he accompanied [James Hay, Lord Doncaster](/wiki/James_Hay,_Lord_Doncaster "James Hay, Lord Doncaster") to France, where he was sent to congratulate [Louis XIII](/wiki/Louis_XIII "Louis XIII") on his marriage, but Hall was compelled by illness to return.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) In his absence, the king nominated him [Dean of Worcester](/wiki/Dean_of_Worcester "Dean of Worcester"), and, in 1617, he accompanied [James](/wiki/James_I_of_England "James I of England") to [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland"), where he defended the [Five Articles of Perth](/wiki/Five_Articles_of_Perth "Five Articles of Perth"), five points of ceremonial which the king desired to impose upon the Scots.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBremerWebster2006117-8)

In the next year Hall was chosen as one of the English deputies at the [Synod of Dort](/wiki/Synod_of_Dort "Synod of Dort").[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) However he fell ill, and was replaced by [Thomas Goad](/wiki/Thomas_Goad "Thomas Goad").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryant2000-9) At the time (1621–1622) when [Marco Antonio de Dominis](/wiki/Marco_Antonio_de_Dominis "Marco Antonio de Dominis") announced his intention to return to Rome, after a stay in England, Hall wrote to try to dissuade him, without success. In a long-unpublished reply (printed 1666) De Dominis justified himself in a comprehensive statement of his mission against [schism](/wiki/Schism_(religion) "Schism (religion)") and its limited results, hampered by Dort and a lack of freedom under James I.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson1997252–253-10)

Career at Exeter and Norwich
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career at Exeter and Norwich")]

In a sermon *Columba Noæ* of February 1624 (1623 [Old Style](/wiki/Old_Style "Old Style")) to Convocation, Hall gave a list or personal panorama of leading theologians of the Church of England.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorwich1808145-11) In the same year he also refused the [see of Gloucester](/wiki/See_of_Gloucester "See of Gloucester"): at the time English delegates to Dort were receiving preferment, since King James approved of the outcome. Hall was then involved as a mediator, taking an active part in the [Arminian and Calvinist controversy in the English church](/wiki/Arminian_and_Calvinist_controversy_in_the_English_church "Arminian and Calvinist controversy in the English church"), and trying to get other clergy to accept Dort. In 1627, he became [Bishop of Exeter](/wiki/Bishop_of_Exeter "Bishop of Exeter").[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189077-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13)

In spite of his Calvinistic opinions, Hall maintained that to acknowledge the errors which had arisen in the Catholic Church did not necessarily imply disbelief in her catholicity, and that the Church of England having repudiated these errors should not deny the claims of the Roman Catholic Church on that account. This view commended itself to [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") and his episcopal advisers; even if Hall, with [John Davenant](/wiki/John_Davenant "John Davenant") and [Thomas Morton](/wiki/Thomas_Morton_(bishop) "Thomas Morton (bishop)"), was considered a likely die-hard by [Richard Montagu](/wiki/Richard_Montagu "Richard Montagu") if it ever came to reunification with the Catholic Church.[[13]](#cite_note-14) At the same time, [Archbishop Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") sent spies into Hall's diocese to report on the Calvinistic tendencies of the bishop and his lenience to the Puritan and low church clergy.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) Hall gradually took up an anti-Laudian, but also anti-[Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") position, while remaining a Protestant [eirenicist](/wiki/Eirenicist "Eirenicist") in co-operation with [John Dury](/wiki/John_Dury "John Dury") and concerned with continental Europe.[[14]](#cite_note-15)

In 1641 Hall was translated to the [See of Norwich](/wiki/See_of_Norwich "See of Norwich"), and in the same year sat on the Lords' Committee on religion. On 30 December, he was, with other bishops, brought before the bar of the [House of Lords](/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords") to answer a charge of [high treason](/wiki/High_treason "High treason") of which the Commons had voted them guilty. They were finally convicted of an offence against the Statute of [Praemunire](/wiki/Praemunire "Praemunire"), and condemned to forfeit their estates, receiving a small maintenance from the parliament. They were immured in [the Tower of London](/wiki/The_Tower_of_London "The Tower of London") from New Year to [Whitsuntide](/wiki/Whitsuntide "Whitsuntide"), when they were released on finding bail.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1)

Retirement
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Retirement")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Dolphin_Inn%2C_Norwich_-_geograph.org.uk_-_182501.jpg/250px-Dolphin_Inn%2C_Norwich_-_geograph.org.uk_-_182501.jpg)](/wiki/File:Dolphin_Inn,_Norwich_-_geograph.org.uk_-_182501.jpg)

The Dolphin Inn, [Norwich](/wiki/Norwich "Norwich"), in the building where Hall had his palace from 1643 to 1647

On his release, Hall proceeded to his new diocese at Norwich, the revenues of which he seems for a time to have received, but in 1643, when the property of the "malignants" was sequestrated, Hall was mentioned by name. He was deprived of his See by Parliament on 9 October 1646, as episcopacy was abolished for the duration of the [Commonwealth](/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") and the [Protectorate](/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate").[[15]](#cite_note-16)[[16]](#cite_note-17) Mrs Hall had difficulty in securing a fifth of the maintenance (£400) assigned to the bishop by the parliament; they were eventually ejected from the palace, and the cathedral was dismantled.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) Hall describes its desecration in *Hard Measure*:

> Lord, what work was here! what clattering of glasses and beating down of walls! what tearing up of monuments! what pulling down of seats! what wrestling down of irons and brass from the windows and walls...[[17]](#cite_note-Hard-18)

Hall described the triumphal procession of the Puritan iconoclasts as they carried vestments, service books and singing books to be burned in the nearby market place, while soldiers lounged in the despoiled cathedral drinking and smoking their pipes.[[17]](#cite_note-Hard-18)

Hall retired to the hamlet of [Heigham](/wiki/Heigham "Heigham"), now a suburb of Norwich, where he spent his last thirteen years preaching and writing until "he was first forbidden by man, and at last disabled by God".[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) In 1655 [Gibson Lucas](/wiki/Gibson_Lucas "Gibson Lucas"), the former [presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") Commissioner and [Justice of the Peace](/wiki/Justice_of_the_Peace "Justice of the Peace") in [Suffolk](/wiki/Suffolk "Suffolk"), regretted his previous rejection of [episcopal polity](/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity"). He was one of 63 priests Hall ordained in contravention of the [9 October 1646 Ordinance for the abolishing of Archbishops and Bishops](/wiki/List_of_Ordinances_and_Acts_of_the_Parliament_of_England,_1642%E2%80%931660#October_1646 "List of Ordinances and Acts of the Parliament of England, 1642–1660"). However Hall regarded Lucas as a "notable precedent for the rest of our learned, & religious Gentry to follow".[[18]](#cite_note-Hall_Olive-tree-19)

He bore his many troubles and the additional burden of much bodily suffering with sweetness and patience, dying on 8 September 1656.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) In his old age, Hall was attended upon by the doctor [Thomas Browne](/wiki/Thomas_Browne "Thomas Browne"), who wrote of him:

> A person of singular humility, patience and piety: his own works are the best monument, and character of himself, which was also very lively drawn in his excellent funeral sermon preached by my learned and faithful friend Mr. John Whitefoot, Rector of Heigham.[[19]](#cite_note-20)

Hall was buried at St Bartholomew, Heigham,[[20]](#cite_note-21) but the church was bombed in 1942, and in 1975 his remains were moved to the cathedral cloisters. The location of the re-burial was then 'forgotten' only to be re-discovered in 2012 by David Berwick using photographs of the ceremony taken for the [Eastern Daily Press](/wiki/Eastern_Daily_Press "Eastern Daily Press").[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-23)

Works
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Works")]

Hall contributed to several distinct literary areas: satirical verse as a young man; polemical writing, particularly in defending [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy "Episcopacy"); and devotional writings, including contemplations carrying a political slant. He was influenced by [Lipsian neostoicism](/wiki/Lipsian_neostoicism "Lipsian neostoicism").[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPapy2004-24) The anonymous *Mundus alter et idem* is a satirical utopian fantasy, not denied by him in strong terms at any point.

### Satire and poetry

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Satire and poetry")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Joseph-Hall-Virgidemiarum-1597.jpg/250px-Joseph-Hall-Virgidemiarum-1597.jpg)](/wiki/File:Joseph-Hall-Virgidemiarum-1597.jpg)

Title page of Joseph Hall's Virgidemiarum, 1597.

During his residence at Cambridge, Hall wrote his *Virgidemiarum* (1597),[[b]](#cite_note-25) satires in English written after Latin models. The claim he put forward in the prologue to be the earliest English satirist:

> I first adventure, follow me who list  
> And be the second English satirist.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)

offended [John Marston](/wiki/John_Marston_(poet) "John Marston (poet)"), who attacked him in satires published in 1598.[[24]](#cite_note-26) In the declining years of the reign of [Elizabeth I](/wiki/Elizabeth_I "Elizabeth I") there was much satirical literature, and it was felt to be an attack on established institutions. [John Whitgift](/wiki/John_Whitgift "John Whitgift"), the [archbishop of Canterbury](/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), ordered that Hall's satires, along with works of [Thomas Nashe](/wiki/Thomas_Nashe "Thomas Nashe"), [John Marston](/wiki/John_Marston_(poet) "John Marston (poet)"), [Christopher Marlowe](/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe "Christopher Marlowe"), [Sir John Davies](/wiki/Sir_John_Davies "Sir John Davies") and others should be burnt, on the ground of licentiousness; but shortly afterwards Hall's book was ordered to be "staied at the press," which may be interpreted as reprieved.[[25]](#cite_note-27)

*Virgidemiarum* was followed by an amended edition in 1598, and in the same year by *Virgidemiarum. The three last bookes. Of byting Satyres* (reprinted 1599). Not in fact the earliest English satirist, Hall wrote in smooth [heroic couplets](/wiki/Heroic_couplet "Heroic couplet"). In the first book of his satires *(Poeticall)*, he attacks the writers whose verses were devoted to licentious subjects, the bombast of *[Tamburlaine](/wiki/Tamburlaine_(play) "Tamburlaine (play)")* and tragedies built on similar lines, the laments of the ghosts of the *[Mirror for Magistrates](/wiki/Mirror_for_Magistrates "Mirror for Magistrates")*, the metrical eccentricities of [Gabriel Harvey](/wiki/Gabriel_Harvey "Gabriel Harvey") and [Richard Stanyhurst](/wiki/Richard_Stanyhurst "Richard Stanyhurst"), the extravagances of the sonneteers, and the sacred poets ([Southwell](/wiki/Robert_Southwell_(Jesuit) "Robert Southwell (Jesuit)") is aimed at in "Now good St Peter weeps pure Helicon, And both the Mary's make a music moan"). In Book II Satire 6 occurs a description of the trencher-chaplain, who is tutor and hanger-on in a country manor. Among his other satirical portraits is that of the famished gallant, the guest of "Duke Humfray." Book VI consists of one long satire on vices and follies dealt with in the earlier books.

Hall's earliest published verse appeared in a collection of elegies on the death of [William Whitaker](/wiki/William_Whitaker_(theologian) "William Whitaker (theologian)"), to which he contributed the only English poem (1596). A line in Marston's *Pigmalion's Image* (1598) indicates that Hall wrote [pastoral poems](/wiki/Pastoral_poem "Pastoral poem"), but none of these have survived,[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189075-5) although his poem 'A Defiance to Envy' has some pastoral elements. He also wrote:

* *The King's Prophecie*; or [*Weeping Joy*](https://archive.org/details/cu31924013279504) (1603), a gratulatory poem on the accession of James I
* *Epistles*, both the first and second volumes of which appeared in 1608 and a third in 1611
* [*Characters of Virtues and Vices*](http://www.luminarium.org/renascence-editions/hallch.htm) (1608), versified by [Nahum Tate](/wiki/Nahum_Tate "Nahum Tate") (1691)
* *Solomon's Divine Arts* (1609)

Hall gave up verse satires and lighter forms of literature when he was ordained a minister in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

### *Mundus alter et idem*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mundus alter et idem")]

Main article: [Mundus alter et idem](/wiki/Mundus_alter_et_idem "Mundus alter et idem")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Hall_Another_World_and_Yet_the_Same_1607_Cornell_CUL_PJM_1009_01.jpg/250px-Hall_Another_World_and_Yet_the_Same_1607_Cornell_CUL_PJM_1009_01.jpg)](/wiki/File:Hall_Another_World_and_Yet_the_Same_1607_Cornell_CUL_PJM_1009_01.jpg)

Map from *Mundus alter et idem*.

Hall is credited with writing the [dystopian](/wiki/Dystopian "Dystopian") novel *Mundus alter et idem sive Terra Australis antehac semper incognita; Longis itineribus peregrini Academici nuperrime illustrata* (1605? and 1607), a satirical description of London, with some criticism of the Roman Catholic Church.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalzman200239-28)

### Controversy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Controversy")]

Hall's initial work of religious controversy was against Protestant [separatists](/wiki/Separatists "Separatists"). In 1608 he had written a letter of remonstrance to [John Robinson](/wiki/John_Robinson_(pastor) "John Robinson (pastor)") and [John Smyth](/wiki/John_Smyth_(Baptist_minister) "John Smyth (Baptist minister)"). Robinson, who had been a beneficed clergyman near [Yarmouth](/wiki/Great_Yarmouth "Great Yarmouth"), had replied in *An Answer to a Censorious Epistle*; and Hall published (1610) *A Common Apology against the Brownists*, a lengthy treatise answering Robinson paragraph by paragraph. It set a style, tight but rich using [animadversion](/wiki/Animadversion "Animadversion"), for Hall's theological writings. Hall criticised Robinson, the future pastor of the *[Mayflower](/wiki/Mayflower "Mayflower")* congregation, alongside [Richard Bernard](/wiki/Richard_Bernard "Richard Bernard") and [John Murton](/wiki/John_Murton_(theologian) "John Murton (theologian)").[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189076-29)[[28]](#cite_note-30)

In Hall's *Via media, The Way of Peace* (1619), he did his best to persuade the two parties (Calvinist and Arminian) to accept a compromise. His later defence of the English Church, and [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy "Episcopacy") as Biblical, entitled *Episcopacy by Divine Right* (1640), was twice revised at Laud's dictation.

* [![icon](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/P_christianity.svg/40px-P_christianity.svg.png)](/wiki/File:P_christianity.svg)[Christianity portal](/wiki/Portal:Christianity "Portal:Christianity")

This was followed by *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament* (1640 and 1641), an eloquent and forceful defence of Hall's order, which produced a retort from the syndicate of Puritan divines, who wrote under the name of [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus"). This was followed by a long controversy to which [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") contributed five pamphlets, virulently attacking Hall and his early satires.

Other controversial writings by Hall include:

* *The Olde Religion: A treatise, wherein is laid downe the true state of the difference betwixt the Reformed and the Romane Church; and the blame of this schisme is cast upon the true Authors* (1628)
* *Columba Noae olivam adferens*, a sermon preached at St Paul's in 1623
* *A Short Answer to the Vindication of Smectymnuus* (1641)
* *A Modest Confutation of (Milton's) Animadversions* (1642).

### Devotional

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Devotional")]

Hall's devotional works include:

* *Holy Observations Lib. I* (1607)
* *Some few of David's Psalmes Metaphrased* (1609)
* *Three Centuries of Meditations and Vowes, Divine and Morall* (1606, 1607, 1609), edited by Charles Sayle
* *The Arte of Divine Meditation* (1607)
* *Contemplations on the Historical Passages of the Old and New Testaments* (1614)
* *Heaven upon Earth, or of True Peace and Tranquillitie of Mind* (1606), reprinted with some of his letters in [John Wesley](/wiki/John_Wesley "John Wesley")'s *Christian Library*, vol. iv. (1819)
* *Occasional Meditations* (1630), edited by his son Robert Hall
* *Henochisme; or a Treatise showing how to walk with God* (1639), translated from Bishop Hall's Latin by Moses Wall
* *The Devout Soul; or Rules of Heavenly Devotion* (1644), often since reprinted
* *The Balm of Gilead* (1646, 1752)
* *Christ Mysticall; or the blessed union of Christ and his Members* (1647), of which General Gordon was a student (reprinted from Gordon's copy, 1893)
* *Susurrium cum Deo* (1659)
* *The Great Mysterie of Godliness* (1650)
* *Resolutions and Decisions of Divers Practicall cases of Conscience* (1649, 1650, 1654).

### Autobiographical

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Autobiographical")]

Hall's autobiographical tracts are *Observations of some Specialities of Divine Providence in the Life of Joseph Hall, Bishop of Norwich, Written with his own hand*, and his *Hard Measure*, reprinted in [Christopher Wordsworth](/wiki/Christopher_Wordsworth "Christopher Wordsworth")'s *Ecclesiastical Biography*.

### Editions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Editions")]

In 1615 Hall published *A Recollection of such treatises as have been published* (1615, 1617, 1621); in 1625 appeared his *Works* (reprinted 1627, 1628, 1634, 1662).

The first complete *Works* appeared in 1808, edited by [Josiah Pratt](/wiki/Josiah_Pratt "Josiah Pratt"). Other editions are by Peter Hall (1837) and by [Philip Wynter](/wiki/Philip_Wynter "Philip Wynter") (1863). See also *Bishop Hall, his Life and Times* (1826), by Rev. John Jones; *Life of Joseph Hall*, by Rev. George Lewis (1886); [Alexander Balloch Grosart](/wiki/Alexander_Balloch_Grosart "Alexander Balloch Grosart"), *The Complete Poems of Joseph Hall* with introductions, etc. (1879); *Satires*, etc. (*Early English Poets*, ed. [Samuel Weller Singer](/wiki/Samuel_Weller_Singer "Samuel Weller Singer"), 1824). Many of Hall's works were translated into French, and some into [Dutch](/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language"), and there have been numerous selections from his devotional works.

Family
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Family")]

In 1603, Hall married Elizabeth (died 27 August 1652), daughter of George Winiffe of [Brettenham](/wiki/Brettenham,_Suffolk "Brettenham, Suffolk"), Suffolk. They had six sons and two daughters. The eldest son, [Robert](/wiki/Robert_Hall_(priest) "Robert Hall (priest)"), D.D. (1605–1667), became [Canon](/wiki/Canon_(priest) "Canon (priest)") of [Exeter](/wiki/Exeter_Cathedral "Exeter Cathedral") in 1629, and [Archdeacon of Cornwall](/wiki/Archdeacon_of_Cornwall "Archdeacon of Cornwall") in 1633.[[29]](#cite_note-31) Joseph, the second son (1607–1669), was registrar of [Exeter Cathedral](/wiki/Exeter_Cathedral "Exeter Cathedral"). [George](/wiki/George_Hall_(bishop_of_Chester) "George Hall (bishop of Chester)"), the third son (1612–1668), became [bishop of Chester](/wiki/Bishop_of_Chester "Bishop of Chester"). Samuel, the fourth son (1616–1674), was sub-dean of Exeter.[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189079-32) It is claimed that his son Richard Hall (1635–1688), emigrated to America in 1670, and patented a large tract of land on each side of the Susquehanna River, about a mile above the mouth of the Ocheraro, just within the limits of Maryland.[[31]](#cite_note-33)

Authorities
-----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Authorities")]

In 1826 John Jones published *Bishop Hall, His Life and Times*.[[32]](#cite_note-34) A recent biography of Joseph Hall is *Bishop Joseph Hall: 1574–1656: A biographical and critical study* by Frank Livingstone Huntley, D.S.Brewer Ltd, Cambridge, 1979.

Criticism of his satires is to be found in [Thomas Warton](/wiki/Thomas_Warton "Thomas Warton")'s *[History of English Poetry](/wiki/The_History_of_English_Poetry "The History of English Poetry")*, vol. iv. pp. 363–409 (ed. Hazlitt, 1871), where a comparison is instituted between Marston and Hall.

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange.\"[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: See also\")]\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Wheeler 2003 p. 273\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-2)** Wheeler 2003 pp. 273–274\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Milton 1953 p. 871\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-1) Wheeler 2003 p. 274\\n5. **[^](#cite_ref-5)** Milton 1953 p. 874\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** Milton 1953 p. 890\\n7. **[^](#cite_ref-7)** Keeble 2003 p. 132\\n8. **[^](#cite_ref-8)** Stevens 1988 p. 268\\n9. **[^](#cite_ref-9)** Wheeler 2003 p. 275\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n* Keeble, N. [g]\")\\n\\nAppearance\\n\\nmove to sidebar\\nhide\\n\\nFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\\n\\nGroup of clergy active in 1641 England\\n\\n**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name \"Pen name\")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan \"Puritan\") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England \"England\") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland \"Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland\"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) \"Thomas Young (1587-1655)\")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.\\n\\nThe name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) \"Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)\"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder \"Edmund Calamy the Elder\"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen \"Matthew Newcomen\"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow \"William Spurstow\"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall\\'s](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton \"John Milton\") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus\\'s reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThis response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.\\n\\nMilton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions \"Animadversions\")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus \"Apology for Smectymnuus\")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Hoover, David L.; Corns, Thomas N. [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge \"Emmanuel College, Cambridge\") |\\n\\n**Joseph Hall** (1 July 1574\\xa0– 8 September 1656) was an [English bishop](/wiki/List_of_bishops_in_the_Church_of_England \"List of bishops in the Church of England\"), [satirist](/wiki/Satire \"Satire\") and [moralist](/wiki/Moralism \"Moralism\"). His contemporaries knew him as a devotional writer, and a high-profile [controversialist](/wiki/Polemic \"Polemic\") of the early 1640s. In church politics, he tended in fact to a middle way.\\n\\n[Thomas Fuller](/wiki/Thomas_Fuller \"Thomas Fuller\") wrote:[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1)\\n\\n> He was commonly called our English Seneca, for the purenesse, plainnesse, and fulnesse of his style. Not unhappy at Controversies, more happy at Comments, very good in his Characters, better in his Sermons, best of all in his Meditations.\\n\\nHall\\'s relationship to the [stoicism](/wiki/Stoicism \"Stoicism\") of the [classical age](/wiki/Classical_antiquity \"Classical antiquity\"), exemplified by [Seneca the Younger](/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger \"Seneca the Younger\"), is still debated, with the importance of [neo-stoicism](/wiki/Neo-stoicism \"Neo-stoicism\") and the influence of the [Flemish](/wiki/Flemish_people \"Flemish people\") philosopher [Justus Lipsius](/wiki/Justus_Lipsius \"Justus Lipsius\") to his work being contested, in contrast to [Christian morality](/wiki/Christian_ethics \"Christian ethics\").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChew19501130–1145-2)\\n\\nEarly life\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Early life\")]\\n\\nJoseph Hall was born at Bristow Park, [Ashby-de-la-Zouch](/wiki/Ashby-de-la-Zouch \"Ashby-de-la-Zouch\"), on 1 July 1574. His father John Hall was employed under [Henry Hastings, 3rd Earl of Huntingdon](/wiki/Henry_Hastings,_3rd_Earl_of_Huntingdon \"Henry Hastings, 3rd Earl of Huntingdon\"), president of the north, and was his deputy at Ashby. His mother was Winifred Bambridge, a strict puritan ([Perry 1890](#CITEREFPerry1890), p.\\xa075),[[a]](#cite_note-3) whom her son compared to St. Monica.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)\\n\\nHall attended [Ashby Grammar School](/wiki/Ashby_Grammar_School \"Ashby Grammar School\"). When he was 15, Mr. Pelset, lecturer at Leicester, a divine of puritan views, offered to take him \"under indentures\" and educate him for the ministry. Just before this arrangement was completed, it came to the knowledge of Nathaniel Gilby, son of [Anthony Gilby](/wiki/Anthony_Gilby \"Anthony Gilby\") and a fellow of [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge \"Emmanuel College, Cambridge\"), who was a friend of the family. Gilby induced Hall\\'s father to send his son to Emmanuel College in 1589. The expense of his education at the university was partly borne by his uncle, Edmund Sleigh. He was elected scholar and afterwards fellow of Emmanuel College (1595), graduating B.A. in 1592 and M.A. in 1596 (B.D. 1603 and D.D. 1612).([Perry 1890](#CITEREFPerry1890), p.\\xa075) Fuller, nearly a contemporary, says that Hall \"passed all his degrees with great applause\".([Perry 1890](#CITEREFPerry1890), p.\\xa075) He obtained a high reputation in the university for scholarship, and read the public rhetoric lecture in the schools for two years with much credit.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189075-5)[[5]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nPriesthood\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Priesthood\")]\\n\\nHaving taken [holy orders](/wiki/Holy_orders \"Holy orders\"), Hall was offered the mastership of [Blundell\\'s School](/wiki/Blundell%27s_School \"Blundell\\'s School\"), [Tiverton](/wiki/Tiverton,_Devon \"Tiverton, Devon\"), but he refused it in favour of the living of [Hawstead](/wiki/Hawstead \"Hawstead\"), Suffolk, to which he was presented (1601) by [Sir Robert Drury](/wiki/Robert_Drury_(17th_century_MP) \"Robert Drury (17th century MP)\"). The appointment was not wholly satisfactory: in his parish Hall had an opponent in a Mr Lilly, whom he describes as a \"witty and bold atheist\",[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) he had to find money to make his house habitable, and he felt that his patron Sir Robert underpaid him. Nevertheless, in 1603, he married Elizabeth Wynniff of Brettenham, Suffolk (see \"[Family](#Family)\" below).[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)\\n\\nIn 1605, Hall travelled abroad for the first time when he accompanied Sir [Edmund Bacon](/wiki/Sir_Edmund_Bacon,_2nd_Baronet,_of_Redgrave \"Sir Edmund Bacon, 2nd Baronet, of Redgrave\") on an embassy to [Spa](/wiki/Spa,_Belgium \"Spa, Belgium\"), with the special aim, he says, of acquainting himself with the state and practice of the Roman Catholic Church. At [Brussels](/wiki/Brussels \"Brussels\"), he disputed at the [Jesuit](/wiki/Jesuit \"Jesuit\") college on the authenticity of modern miracles, until his patron at length asked him to stop.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)\\n\\nHall\\'s devotional writings had attracted the notice of [Henry, Prince of Wales](/wiki/Henry_Frederick,_Prince_of_Wales \"Henry Frederick, Prince of Wales\"), who made him one of his chaplains (1608).[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) Hall preached officially on the tenth anniversary of [King James\\'s](/wiki/James_VI_and_I \"James VI and I\") accession in 1613, with an assessment in *An Holy Panegyrick* of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\") flattering to the king.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParry1981232–235-7)\\n\\nIn 1612, [Edward Denny](/wiki/Edward_Denny,_1st_Earl_of_Norwich \"Edward Denny, 1st Earl of Norwich\") gave Hall the [curacy](/wiki/Curacy \"Curacy\") of [Waltham Holy Cross](/wiki/Waltham_Holy_Cross \"Waltham Holy Cross\"), Essex, and, in the same year, he received the degree of [D.D.](/wiki/D.D. \"D.D.\") Later he received the [prebend](/wiki/Prebendary \"Prebendary\") of [Willenhall](/wiki/Willenhall \"Willenhall\") in [St Peter\\'s](/wiki/St_Peter%27s_Collegiate_Church \"St Peter\\'s Collegiate Church\"), the [collegiate church](/wiki/Collegiate_church \"Collegiate church\") of [Wolverhampton](/wiki/Wolverhampton \"Wolverhampton\"), and, in 1616, he accompanied [James Hay, Lord Doncaster](/wiki/James_Hay,_Lord_Doncaster \"James Hay, Lord Doncaster\") to France, where he was sent to congratulate [Louis XIII](/wiki/Louis_XIII \"Louis XIII\") on his marriage, but Hall was compelled by illness to return.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) In his absence, the king nominated him [Dean of Worcester](/wiki/Dean_of_Worcester \"Dean of Worcester\"), and, in 1617, he accompanied [James](/wiki/James_I_of_England \"James I of England\") to [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland \"Scotland\"), where he defended the [Five Articles of Perth](/wiki/Five_Articles_of_Perth \"Five Articles of Perth\"), five points of ceremonial which the king desired to impose upon the Scots.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBremerWebster2006117-8)\\n\\nIn the next year Hall was chosen as one of the English deputies at the [Synod of Dort](/wiki/Synod_of_Dort \"Synod of Dort\").[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4) However he fell ill, and was replaced by [Thomas Goad](/wiki/Thomas_Goad \"Thomas Goad\").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryant2000-9) At the time (1621–1622) when [Marco Antonio de Dominis](/wiki/Marco_Antonio_de_Dominis \"Marco Antonio de Dominis\") announced his intention to return to Rome, after a stay in England, Hall wrote to try to dissuade him, without success. In a long-unpublished reply (printed 1666) De Dominis justified himself in a comprehensive statement of his mission against [schism](/wiki/Schism_(religion) \"Schism (religion)\") and its limited results, hampered by Dort and a lack of freedom under James I.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson1997252–253-10)\\n\\nCareer at Exeter and Norwich\\n----------------------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Career at Exeter and Norwich\")]\\n\\nIn a sermon *Columba Noæ* of February 1624 (1623 [Old Style](/wiki/Old_Style \"Old Style\")) to Convocation, Hall gave a list or personal panorama of leading theologians of the Church of England.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorwich1808145-11) In the same year he also refused the [see of Gloucester](/wiki/See_of_Gloucester \"See of Gloucester\"): at the time English delegates to Dort were receiving preferment, since King James approved of the outcome. Hall was then involved as a mediator, taking an active part in the [Arminian and Calvinist controversy in the English church](/wiki/Arminian_and_Calvinist_controversy_in_the_English_church \"Arminian and Calvinist controversy in the English church\"), and trying to get other clergy to accept Dort. In 1627, he became [Bishop of Exeter](/wiki/Bishop_of_Exeter \"Bishop of Exeter\").[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189077-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13)\\n\\nIn spite of his Calvinistic opinions, Hall maintained that to acknowledge the errors which had arisen in the Catholic Church did not necessarily imply disbelief in her catholicity, and that the Church of England having repudiated these errors should not deny the claims of the Roman Catholic Church on that account. This view commended itself to [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\") and his episcopal advisers; even if Hall, with [John Davenant](/wiki/John_Davenant \"John Davenant\") and [Thomas Morton](/wiki/Thomas_Morton_(bishop) \"Thomas Morton (bishop)\"), was considered a likely die-hard by [Richard Montagu](/wiki/Richard_Montagu \"Richard Montagu\") if it ever came to reunification with the Catholic Church.[[13]](#cite_note-14) At the same time, [Archbishop Laud](/wiki/William_Laud \"William Laud\") sent spies into Hall\\'s diocese to report on the Calvinistic tendencies of the bishop and his lenience to the Puritan and low church clergy.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) Hall gradually took up an anti-Laudian, but also anti-[Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian \"Presbyterian\") position, while remaining a Protestant [eirenicist](/wiki/Eirenicist \"Eirenicist\") in co-operation with [John Dury](/wiki/John_Dury \"John Dury\") and concerned with continental Europe.[[14]](#cite_note-15)\\n\\nIn 1641 Hall was translated to the [See of Norwich](/wiki/See_of_Norwich \"See of Norwich\"), and in the same year sat on the Lords\\' Committee on religion. On 30 December, he was, with other bishops, brought before the bar of the [House of Lords](/wiki/House_of_Lords \"House of Lords\") to answer a charge of [high treason](/wiki/High_treason \"High treason\") of which the Commons had voted them guilty. They were finally convicted of an offence against the Statute of [Praemunire](/wiki/Praemunire \"Praemunire\"), and condemned to forfeit their estates, receiving a small maintenance from the parliament. They were immured in [the Tower of London](/wiki/The_Tower_of_London \"The Tower of London\") from New Year to [Whitsuntide](/wiki/Whitsuntide \"Whitsuntide\"), when they were released on finding bail.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1)\\n\\nRetirement\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: Retirement\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Dolphin_Inn%2C_Norwich_-_geograph.org.uk_-_182501.jpg/250px-Dolphin_Inn%2C_Norwich_-_geograph.org.uk_-_182501.jpg)](/wiki/File:Dolphin_Inn,_Norwich_-_geograph.org.uk_-_182501.jpg)\\n\\nThe Dolphin Inn, [Norwich](/wiki/Norwich \"Norwich\"), in the building where Hall had his palace from 1643 to 1647\\n\\nOn his release, Hall proceeded to his new diocese at Norwich, the revenues of which he seems for a time to have received, but in 1643, when the property of the \"malignants\" was sequestrated, Hall was mentioned by name. He was deprived of his See by Parliament on 9 October 1646, as episcopacy was abolished for the duration of the [Commonwealth](/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England \"Commonwealth of England\") and the [Protectorate](/wiki/The_Protectorate \"The Protectorate\").[[15]](#cite_note-16)[[16]](#cite_note-17) Mrs Hall had difficulty in securing a fifth of the maintenance (£400) assigned to the bishop by the parliament; they were eventually ejected from the palace, and the cathedral was dismantled.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) Hall describes its desecration in *Hard Measure*:\\n\\n> Lord, what work was here! what clattering of glasses and beating down of walls! what tearing up of monuments! what pulling down of seats! what wrestling down of irons and brass from the windows and walls...[[17]](#cite_note-Hard-18)\\n\\nHall described the triumphal procession of the Puritan iconoclasts as they carried vestments, service books and singing books to be burned in the nearby market place, while soldiers lounged in the despoiled cathedral drinking and smoking their pipes.[[17]](#cite_note-Hard-18)\\n\\nHall retired to the hamlet of [Heigham](/wiki/Heigham \"Heigham\"), now a suburb of Norwich, where he spent his last thirteen years preaching and writing until \"he was first forbidden by man, and at last disabled by God\".[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) In 1655 [Gibson Lucas](/wiki/Gibson_Lucas \"Gibson Lucas\"), the former [presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian \"Presbyterian\") Commissioner and [Justice of the Peace](/wiki/Justice_of_the_Peace \"Justice of the Peace\") in [Suffolk](/wiki/Suffolk \"Suffolk\"), regretted his previous rejection of [episcopal polity](/wiki/Episcopal_polity \"Episcopal polity\"). He was one of 63 priests Hall ordained in contravention of the [9 October 1646 Ordinance for the abolishing of Archbishops and Bishops](/wiki/List_of_Ordinances_and_Acts_of_the_Parliament_of_England,_1642%E2%80%931660#October_1646 \"List of Ordinances and Acts of the Parliament of England, 1642–1660\"). However Hall regarded Lucas as a \"notable precedent for the rest of our learned, & religious Gentry to follow\".[[18]](#cite_note-Hall_Olive-tree-19)\\n\\nHe bore his many troubles and the additional burden of much bodily suffering with sweetness and patience, dying on 8 September 1656.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911848-1) In his old age, Hall was attended upon by the doctor [Thomas Browne](/wiki/Thomas_Browne \"Thomas Browne\"), who wrote of him:\\n\\n> A person of singular humility, patience and piety: his own works are the best monument, and character of himself, which was also very lively drawn in his excellent funeral sermon preached by my learned and faithful friend Mr. John Whitefoot, Rector of Heigham.[[19]](#cite_note-20)\\n\\nHall was buried at St Bartholomew, Heigham,[[20]](#cite_note-21) but the church was bombed in 1942, and in 1975 his remains were moved to the cathedral cloisters. The location of the re-burial was then \\'forgotten\\' only to be re-discovered in 2012 by David Berwick using photographs of the ceremony taken for the [Eastern Daily Press](/wiki/Eastern_Daily_Press \"Eastern Daily Press\").[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-23)\\n\\nWorks\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Works\")]\\n\\nHall contributed to several distinct literary areas: satirical verse as a young man; polemical writing, particularly in defending [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy \"Episcopacy\"); and devotional writings, including contemplations carrying a political slant. He was influenced by [Lipsian neostoicism](/wiki/Lipsian_neostoicism \"Lipsian neostoicism\").[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPapy2004-24) The anonymous *Mundus alter et idem* is a satirical utopian fantasy, not denied by him in strong terms at any point.\\n\\n### Satire and poetry\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: Satire and poetry\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Joseph-Hall-Virgidemiarum-1597.jpg/250px-Joseph-Hall-Virgidemiarum-1597.jpg)](/wiki/File:Joseph-Hall-Virgidemiarum-1597.jpg)\\n\\nTitle page of Joseph Hall\\'s Virgidemiarum, 1597.\\n\\nDuring his residence at Cambridge, Hall wrote his *Virgidemiarum* (1597),[[b]](#cite_note-25) satires in English written after Latin models. The claim he put forward in the prologue to be the earliest English satirist:\\n\\n> I first adventure, follow me who list  \\n> And be the second English satirist.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911847-4)\\n\\noffended [John Marston](/wiki/John_Marston_(poet) \"John Marston (poet)\"), who attacked him in satires published in 1598.[[24]](#cite_note-26) In the declining years of the reign of [Elizabeth I](/wiki/Elizabeth_I \"Elizabeth I\") there was much satirical literature, and it was felt to be an attack on established institutions. [John Whitgift](/wiki/John_Whitgift \"John Whitgift\"), the [archbishop of Canterbury](/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury \"Archbishop of Canterbury\"), ordered that Hall\\'s satires, along with works of [Thomas Nashe](/wiki/Thomas_Nashe \"Thomas Nashe\"), [John Marston](/wiki/John_Marston_(poet) \"John Marston (poet)\"), [Christopher Marlowe](/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe \"Christopher Marlowe\"), [Sir John Davies](/wiki/Sir_John_Davies \"Sir John Davies\") and others should be burnt, on the ground of licentiousness; but shortly afterwards Hall\\'s book was ordered to be \"staied at the press,\" which may be interpreted as reprieved.[[25]](#cite_note-27)\\n\\n*Virgidemiarum* was followed by an amended edition in 1598, and in the same year by *Virgidemiarum. The three last bookes. Of byting Satyres* (reprinted 1599). Not in fact the earliest English satirist, Hall wrote in smooth [heroic couplets](/wiki/Heroic_couplet \"Heroic couplet\"). In the first book of his satires *(Poeticall)*, he attacks the writers whose verses were devoted to licentious subjects, the bombast of *[Tamburlaine](/wiki/Tamburlaine_(play) \"Tamburlaine (play)\")* and tragedies built on similar lines, the laments of the ghosts of the *[Mirror for Magistrates](/wiki/Mirror_for_Magistrates \"Mirror for Magistrates\")*, the metrical eccentricities of [Gabriel Harvey](/wiki/Gabriel_Harvey \"Gabriel Harvey\") and [Richard Stanyhurst](/wiki/Richard_Stanyhurst \"Richard Stanyhurst\"), the extravagances of the sonneteers, and the sacred poets ([Southwell](/wiki/Robert_Southwell_(Jesuit) \"Robert Southwell (Jesuit)\") is aimed at in \"Now good St Peter weeps pure Helicon, And both the Mary\\'s make a music moan\"). In Book II Satire 6 occurs a description of the trencher-chaplain, who is tutor and hanger-on in a country manor. Among his other satirical portraits is that of the famished gallant, the guest of \"Duke Humfray.\" Book VI consists of one long satire on vices and follies dealt with in the earlier books.\\n\\nHall\\'s earliest published verse appeared in a collection of elegies on the death of [William Whitaker](/wiki/William_Whitaker_(theologian) \"William Whitaker (theologian)\"), to which he contributed the only English poem (1596). A line in Marston\\'s *Pigmalion\\'s Image* (1598) indicates that Hall wrote [pastoral poems](/wiki/Pastoral_poem \"Pastoral poem\"), but none of these have survived,[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189075-5) although his poem \\'A Defiance to Envy\\' has some pastoral elements. He also wrote:\\n\\n* *The King\\'s Prophecie*; or [*Weeping Joy*](https://archive.org/details/cu31924013279504) (1603), a gratulatory poem on the accession of James I\\n* *Epistles*, both the first and second volumes of which appeared in 1608 and a third in 1611\\n* [*Characters of Virtues and Vices*](http://www.luminarium.org/renascence-editions/hallch.htm) (1608), versified by [Nahum Tate](/wiki/Nahum_Tate \"Nahum Tate\") (1691)\\n* *Solomon\\'s Divine Arts* (1609)\\n\\nHall gave up verse satires and lighter forms of literature when he was ordained a minister in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\n### *Mundus alter et idem*\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=7 \"Edit section: Mundus alter et idem\")]\\n\\nMain article: [Mundus alter et idem](/wiki/Mundus_alter_et_idem \"Mundus alter et idem\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Hall_Another_World_and_Yet_the_Same_1607_Cornell_CUL_PJM_1009_01.jpg/250px-Hall_Another_World_and_Yet_the_Same_1607_Cornell_CUL_PJM_1009_01.jpg)](/wiki/File:Hall_Another_World_and_Yet_the_Same_1607_Cornell_CUL_PJM_1009_01.jpg)\\n\\nMap from *Mundus alter et idem*.\\n\\nHall is credited with writing the [dystopian](/wiki/Dystopian \"Dystopian\") novel *Mundus alter et idem sive Terra Australis antehac semper incognita; Longis itineribus peregrini Academici nuperrime illustrata* (1605? and 1607), a satirical description of London, with some criticism of the Roman Catholic Church.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalzman200239-28)\\n\\n### Controversy\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=8 \"Edit section: Controversy\")]\\n\\nHall\\'s initial work of religious controversy was against Protestant [separatists](/wiki/Separatists \"Separatists\"). In 1608 he had written a letter of remonstrance to [John Robinson](/wiki/John_Robinson_(pastor) \"John Robinson (pastor)\") and [John Smyth](/wiki/John_Smyth_(Baptist_minister) \"John Smyth (Baptist minister)\"). Robinson, who had been a beneficed clergyman near [Yarmouth](/wiki/Great_Yarmouth \"Great Yarmouth\"), had replied in *An Answer to a Censorious Epistle*; and Hall published (1610) *A Common Apology against the Brownists*, a lengthy treatise answering Robinson paragraph by paragraph. It set a style, tight but rich using [animadversion](/wiki/Animadversion \"Animadversion\"), for Hall\\'s theological writings. Hall criticised Robinson, the future pastor of the *[Mayflower](/wiki/Mayflower \"Mayflower\")* congregation, alongside [Richard Bernard](/wiki/Richard_Bernard \"Richard Bernard\") and [John Murton](/wiki/John_Murton_(theologian) \"John Murton (theologian)\").[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189076-29)[[28]](#cite_note-30)\\n\\nIn Hall\\'s *Via media, The Way of Peace* (1619), he did his best to persuade the two parties (Calvinist and Arminian) to accept a compromise. His later defence of the English Church, and [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy \"Episcopacy\") as Biblical, entitled *Episcopacy by Divine Right* (1640), was twice revised at Laud\\'s dictation.\\n\\n* [![icon](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/P_christianity.svg/40px-P_christianity.svg.png)](/wiki/File:P_christianity.svg)[Christianity portal](/wiki/Portal:Christianity \"Portal:Christianity\")\\n\\nThis was followed by *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament* (1640 and 1641), an eloquent and forceful defence of Hall\\'s order, which produced a retort from the syndicate of Puritan divines, who wrote under the name of [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\"). This was followed by a long controversy to which [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton \"John Milton\") contributed five pamphlets, virulently attacking Hall and his early satires.\\n\\nOther controversial writings by Hall include:\\n\\n* *The Olde Religion: A treatise, wherein is laid downe the true state of the difference betwixt the Reformed and the Romane Church; and the blame of this schisme is cast upon the true Authors* (1628)\\n* *Columba Noae olivam adferens*, a sermon preached at St Paul\\'s in 1623\\n* *A Short Answer to the Vindication of Smectymnuus* (1641)\\n* *A Modest Confutation of (Milton\\'s) Animadversions* (1642).\\n\\n### Devotional\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=9 \"Edit section: Devotional\")]\\n\\nHall\\'s devotional works include:\\n\\n* *Holy Observations Lib. I* (1607)\\n* *Some few of David\\'s Psalmes Metaphrased* (1609)\\n* *Three Centuries of Meditations and Vowes, Divine and Morall* (1606, 1607, 1609), edited by Charles Sayle\\n* *The Arte of Divine Meditation* (1607)\\n* *Contemplations on the Historical Passages of the Old and New Testaments* (1614)\\n* *Heaven upon Earth, or of True Peace and Tranquillitie of Mind* (1606), reprinted with some of his letters in [John Wesley](/wiki/John_Wesley \"John Wesley\")\\'s *Christian Library*, vol. iv. (1819)\\n* *Occasional Meditations* (1630), edited by his son Robert Hall\\n* *Henochisme; or a Treatise showing how to walk with God* (1639), translated from Bishop Hall\\'s Latin by Moses Wall\\n* *The Devout Soul; or Rules of Heavenly Devotion* (1644), often since reprinted\\n* *The Balm of Gilead* (1646, 1752)\\n* *Christ Mysticall; or the blessed union of Christ and his Members* (1647), of which General Gordon was a student (reprinted from Gordon\\'s copy, 1893)\\n* *Susurrium cum Deo* (1659)\\n* *The Great Mysterie of Godliness* (1650)\\n* *Resolutions and Decisions of Divers Practicall cases of Conscience* (1649, 1650, 1654).\\n\\n### Autobiographical\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=10 \"Edit section: Autobiographical\")]\\n\\nHall\\'s autobiographical tracts are *Observations of some Specialities of Divine Providence in the Life of Joseph Hall, Bishop of Norwich, Written with his own hand*, and his *Hard Measure*, reprinted in [Christopher Wordsworth](/wiki/Christopher_Wordsworth \"Christopher Wordsworth\")\\'s *Ecclesiastical Biography*.\\n\\n### Editions\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=11 \"Edit section: Editions\")]\\n\\nIn 1615 Hall published *A Recollection of such treatises as have been published* (1615, 1617, 1621); in 1625 appeared his *Works* (reprinted 1627, 1628, 1634, 1662).\\n\\nThe first complete *Works* appeared in 1808, edited by [Josiah Pratt](/wiki/Josiah_Pratt \"Josiah Pratt\"). Other editions are by Peter Hall (1837) and by [Philip Wynter](/wiki/Philip_Wynter \"Philip Wynter\") (1863). See also *Bishop Hall, his Life and Times* (1826), by Rev. John Jones; *Life of Joseph Hall*, by Rev. George Lewis (1886); [Alexander Balloch Grosart](/wiki/Alexander_Balloch_Grosart \"Alexander Balloch Grosart\"), *The Complete Poems of Joseph Hall* with introductions, etc. (1879); *Satires*, etc. (*Early English Poets*, ed. [Samuel Weller Singer](/wiki/Samuel_Weller_Singer \"Samuel Weller Singer\"), 1824). Many of Hall\\'s works were translated into French, and some into [Dutch](/wiki/Dutch_language \"Dutch language\"), and there have been numerous selections from his devotional works.\\n\\nFamily\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=12 \"Edit section: Family\")]\\n\\nIn 1603, Hall married Elizabeth (died 27 August 1652), daughter of George Winiffe of [Brettenham](/wiki/Brettenham,_Suffolk \"Brettenham, Suffolk\"), Suffolk. They had six sons and two daughters. The eldest son, [Robert](/wiki/Robert_Hall_(priest) \"Robert Hall (priest)\"), D.D. (1605–1667), became [Canon](/wiki/Canon_(priest) \"Canon (priest)\") of [Exeter](/wiki/Exeter_Cathedral \"Exeter Cathedral\") in 1629, and [Archdeacon of Cornwall](/wiki/Archdeacon_of_Cornwall \"Archdeacon of Cornwall\") in 1633.[[29]](#cite_note-31) Joseph, the second son (1607–1669), was registrar of [Exeter Cathedral](/wiki/Exeter_Cathedral \"Exeter Cathedral\"). [George](/wiki/George_Hall_(bishop_of_Chester) \"George Hall (bishop of Chester)\"), the third son (1612–1668), became [bishop of Chester](/wiki/Bishop_of_Chester \"Bishop of Chester\"). Samuel, the fourth son (1616–1674), was sub-dean of Exeter.[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry189079-32) It is claimed that his son Richard Hall (1635–1688), emigrated to America in 1670, and patented a large tract of land on each side of the Susquehanna River, about a mile above the mouth of the Ocheraro, just within the limits of Maryland.[[31]](#cite_note-33)\\n\\nAuthorities\\n-----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=13 \"Edit section: Authorities\")]\\n\\nIn 1826 John Jones published *Bishop Hall, His Life and Times*.[[32]](#cite_note-34) A recent biography of Joseph Hall is *Bishop Joseph Hall: 1574–1656: A biographical and critical study* by Frank Livingstone Huntley, D.S.Brewer Ltd, Cambridge, 1979.\\n\\nCriticism of his satires is to be found in [Thomas Warton](/wiki/Thomas_Warton \"Thomas Warton\")\\'s *[History of English Poetry](/wiki/The_History_of_English_Poetry \"The History of English Poetry\")*, vol. iv. pp.\\xa0363–409 (ed. Hazlitt, 1871), where a comparison is instituted between Marston and Hall.\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Joseph_Hall_(bishop)&action=edit&section=14 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Hall has left among his works two tracts (\"Observations of some Specialties of Divine Providence in the Life of Joseph Hall, Bishop of Norwich\", and \"Hard Measure\"), which together form a useful and interesting autobiography ([Perry 1890](#CITEREFPerry1890), p.\\xa075).\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-25)** \"Virgidemiarum. ***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)
